clue.text: Students here affected America

blocks.note: camp means theatrically affected or exaggerated in manner
US is the standard abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: Students somewhere have made a lasting impression on America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' looks like a verb meaning influenced, but it is the adjective meaning mannered or theatrical.
explanation.definitionFit: A university's grounds and buildings are where its students live, attend lectures and spend their days.

clue.text: Range of adult records from former times

blocks.note: A is the film-classification abbreviation for adult
LPs are long-playing vinyl records, a format of earlier decades

explanation.surface: A collection of grown-up music recordings from years gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' reads like a selection of goods, but it is a mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: The great European mountain chain stretching across Switzerland, Austria, France and Italy is a classic example of a range.

clue.text: Soldiers, with one jerk clinging on for support

blocks.note: paras are paratroopers
I is the Roman numeral one
a tic is an involuntary twitch or jerk

explanation.surface: Troops, one of them a fool, holding on to each other for help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jerk' suggests an idiot, but it means a twitch here.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasite lives by attaching itself to a host and drawing sustenance, so dependent hanging-on fits the adjective.

clue.text: Labour needs a new election catchphrase?

blocks.note: slog is hard work, toil
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: The Labour Party wants a fresh campaign soundbite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' is capitalised to suggest the British political party, but it just means hard work. The question mark flags that the definition is an example, as slogans are not only for elections.
explanation.definitionFit: A short memorable phrase used in campaigning or advertising is exactly what a political party's catchphrase is.

clue.text: Tom possibly on a search for dead accommodating place

indicators.note: one thing sitting on another means the first is placed against the second, side by side

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat, so 'possibly' marks an example
taken as written
to comb an area is to search it thoroughly

explanation.surface: A tomcat hunting for a sheltered spot for a dead body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom possibly' is a definition by example: a tom is one kind of cat.
explanation.definitionFit: An underground cemetery with burial niches in tunnels is a place built to house the bodies of the dead.

clue.text: Customer is e.g. about to be covered in blubber as a means of improving looks?

indicators.note: 'about' suggests moving around, so these letters are turned into a new order
something covered in another is wrapped inside it, so one group goes within another

blocks.note: the letters of these three words are the raw material
to blubber is to cry noisily

explanation.surface: A client is about to be swaddled in fat, which is a strange way to look better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blubber' suggests whale fat, fitting the beauty theme, but it means weep. The jumbled twelve letters sit between C and RY.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgical procedures such as facelifts and nose jobs are performed mainly to change and enhance a person's appearance.

clue.text: Bugs, garden tools, dance wear

blocks.note: to bug a phone is to tap it
hoes are weeding tools

explanation.surface: A list of things you might find in a shed: insects, garden implements and costumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' looks like insects, but it is the verb for secretly listening in.
explanation.definitionFit: Footwear with metal plates on the soles, worn by tap dancers to make rhythmic sounds, is clothing for dancing.

clue.text: Garnish shows one’s out of touch romantically

indicators.note: when something is out of a place it has left, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: A means one, as in 'a single'
a caress is a loving touch

explanation.surface: A garnish reveals that someone has lost their romantic touch.
explanation.walkthrough: Take A, meaning one, out of CARESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Small peppery salad leaves are often scattered on a plate as a decoration or garnish for food.

clue.text: Could be Ludlow’s ATM network needs fixing

indicators.note: something that needs fixing is broken and must be put back together in a different shape

blocks.note: the letters of these two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: The cash machines in a small Shropshire town are out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: Ludlow is a historic town in Shropshire, England, famous for its market. 'Could be' marks it as an example; the ’s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An English settlement granted the right to hold a regular market, such as Ludlow, is the general category named.

clue.text: Dodgy football club concealing debt

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hide it inside, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur, a London football club
an IOU is a written note acknowledging a debt

explanation.surface: A shady football club is hiding what it owes.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur, a Premier League football club in north London; an IOU is a signed note promising repayment.
explanation.definitionFit: Something false or not genuine, though appearing so, can be described informally as suspect or of doubtful honesty.

clue.text: Lines of type or squiggles

indicators.note: squiggles are twisting wavy marks, so the letters are bent into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the letters of these two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: Rows of printed characters or wiggly handwriting on a page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines of type' looks like a printing phrase, but 'Lines' alone is the definition and 'of' the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse is written and recited in lines, so a poem's lines stand for the literary form itself.

clue.text: Before gossip, stand aside

indicators.note: 'before' places one item ahead of the other in reading order

blocks.note: to stage is to put on or stand an event
a whisper is a rumour or piece of gossip

explanation.surface: Someone stepping away before a chat turns to tittle-tattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stand aside' looks like one phrase meaning step back, but 'aside' is the definition, a theatrical term. The stand goes before the gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: In theatre, a remark spoken to the audience that other characters supposedly cannot hear is a loud whisper meant to be overheard.

clue.text: Bird needs a shot to move gracefully

blocks.note: a swan is a large water bird
taken as written
a round is a single shot of ammunition

explanation.surface: A bird must be fired at to make it take flight elegantly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' suggests an attempt or a photograph, but here it is a round of ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: To glide about in a leisurely, showy way, like the elegant water bird, is to drift with poise.

clue.text: Backward Yanks study!?

indicators.note: backward means facing the other way, so the letters run from end to start

blocks.note: to yank is to pull sharply, as a vehicle tows

explanation.surface: An exclamation that Americans are slow learners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yanks' is capitalised to look like Americans, but it is the verb pull. A swot is British slang for someone who studies hard, and to swot is to cram.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage, to revise intensively for an exam is to cram, which matches the verb meaning to learn.

clue.text: What makes the real you deny it – twice, brazenly?

indicators.note: acting brazenly is shameless and wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
the two-letter word written two times

explanation.surface: Shamelessly denying something twice over says a lot about who you really are.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'twice' doubles only the 'it', so the fodder is DENY plus IT IT.
explanation.definitionFit: The set of characteristics that distinguish a person and constitute their true self is what selfhood means.

clue.text: Sort of trifle that produces tight coat!

blocks.note: tight is slang for drunk
to cake is to coat thickly, as with mud

explanation.surface: A dessert so boozy it leaves a snug layer on you.
explanation.walkthrough: A trifle is a British layered pudding of sponge, fruit, custard and cream; a tipsy cake is a similar sponge soaked in wine or sherry. 'tight' and 'coat' look like clothing words.
explanation.definitionFit: This old-fashioned dessert of alcohol-soaked sponge with custard is a close relative of the layered pudding.

clue.text: French writer’s not entirely over LA – “inexorable!”

indicators.note: not entirely means only part is used, so the letters come from inside the words

blocks.note: the letters run on across these words

explanation.surface: A French author is only partly over Los Angeles, which proves relentless.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the second letter of 'over' to the start of 'inexorable'. Paul Verlaine was a nineteenth-century French Symbolist poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Verlaine, the Symbolist poet famous for his stormy relationship with Rimbaud, is a celebrated literary figure from France.

clue.text: Underwear that’s exasperating

definitions.note: the answer is an exclamation used when exasperated, not an adjective

blocks.note: first meaning: women's pants or briefs
second meaning: a British exclamation of annoyance

explanation.surface: Some undergarments are really irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, 'knickers!' is a mild exclamation of annoyance, like 'damn!'; knickers are also women's underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: The garment is women's briefs, and the same word shouted aloud is a mild British expletive of irritation or frustration.

clue.text: Catch wife in embrace of mate

indicators.note: to be in someone's embrace is to be held within their arms, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: pal is a friend or mate
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Seeing one's wife being hugged by a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' looks like a verb meaning to discover, but it is a noun: a pawl is the pivoting catch in a ratchet that stops it slipping back.
explanation.definitionFit: A pivoted bar that engages the teeth of a ratchet wheel to prevent reverse motion is a mechanical stopping device.

clue.text: Sucker’s base program error

blocks.note: a bed is a base or foundation, as in a bed of gravel
a bug is a fault in software

explanation.surface: A gullible person's fundamental software fault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucker' suggests a dupe, but it is literal: this insect sucks blood.
explanation.definitionFit: This small wingless insect feeds by drawing blood from sleeping people, so it is quite literally a bloodsucker.

clue.text: Crime of old lady: nabbing rocking cradle

indicators.note: rocking means swaying to and fro, so the letters are shaken into a new order
to nab is to grab and hold, so one piece takes another inside it

blocks.note: a granny is an old woman, a grandmother
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly woman's offence was snatching a swinging baby's bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocking cradle' sounds like a nursery scene, but 'rocking' scrambles the cradle and the result goes inside GRANNY.
explanation.definitionFit: Theft of property above a set value is classed in some legal systems as a serious felony, a major stealing offence.

clue.text: Nosy overseer of missions by lake

indicators.note: 'by' means next to, so one piece stands beside the other

blocks.note: NASA is the US space agency that runs space missions
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: An inquisitive supervisor of missionaries beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nosy' looks like prying, but it means relating to the nose; 'missions' suggests church work, but they are space flights.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything pertaining to the nose, such as a passage or a voice, can be described with this anatomical adjective.

clue.text: Pound to go out of business

blocks.note: first meaning: an enclosure for animals, especially sheep
second meaning: to collapse as a company

explanation.surface: Losing money until the firm shuts down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like money, fitting the business surface, but it is a pen for livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheep pen is an enclosure for animals, and a company that fails and closes has collapsed like folded cards.

clue.text: Use milk, almost curdled, for breakfast?

definitions.note: the definition describes when the food is eaten rather than naming it

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
something curdled has gone off and separated, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Pouring milk that has nearly gone off on your morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curdled' sounds like the milk going sour, but it scrambles the letters of USE and a shortened milk.
explanation.definitionFit: This Swiss mix of oats, nuts and dried fruit is a cereal typically eaten in the morning meal.

clue.text: Display lamb cooked in controlled zone

indicators.note: cooked means prepared and altered, so the letters are rearranged
to control is to direct and manage, so these letters are marshalled into a fresh order
in places one item inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Showing off lamb roasted in a regulated area.
explanation.walkthrough: Both four-letter words are rearranged, then the reworked lamb goes inside the reworked zone after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To emblazon is to decorate conspicuously, as with a heraldic device, so it means to show or exhibit prominently.

clue.text: Mature blend of rye? That’s cheating!

indicators.note: a blend mixes things together, so the letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: mature means grown up
taken as written

explanation.surface: An aged whisky blend is a fraud on the drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mature blend of rye' reads like whisky talk; rye is a whisky, but here only its letters are mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unfaithful to one's spouse by having sex with someone else is infidelity, colloquially called being a cheat.

clue.text: Good as a woodwind section – but insatiable

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
woodwind instruments use reeds, so the section is full of reeds

explanation.surface: An orchestra's woodwind players are skilled but never satisfied.
explanation.walkthrough: Oboes, clarinets and bassoons are reed instruments, so a woodwind section might be called reedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who always wants more food or wealth and can never be satisfied has an excessive appetite.
